B59-000: A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.
This is the founding document of the vault. Every other record here is a precursor to it, a parallel lineage that fed it, or a consequence that followed from it.

Nine pages, posted to the Cryptography Mailing List on 31 October 2008 by a pseudonymous author, "Satoshi Nakamoto". It proposes a purely peer-to-peer electronic cash system in which the double-spending problem is solved without any trusted third party: transactions are timestamped by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work, and the longest such chain represents both the majority decision and the record that is computationally hardest to rewrite.

The canonical PDF is the one released and served by bitcoin.org, which distributes it under the MIT licence. Its SHA-256 is recorded below and can be reproduced with sha256sum bitcoin.pdf . A snapshot of the bitcoin.org/en/bitcoin-paper landing page is archived alongside it.

A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution. Digital signatures provide part of the solution, but the main benefits are lost if a trusted third party is still required to prevent double-spending. We propose a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network. The network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work, forming a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof-of-work. The longest chain not only serves as proof of the sequence of events witnessed, but proof that it came from the largest pool of CPU power. As long as a majority of CPU power is controlled by nodes that are not cooperating to attack the network, they'll generate the longest chain and outpace attackers. The network itself requires minimal structure. Messages are broadcast on a best effort basis, and nodes can leave and rejoin the network at will, accepting the longest proof-of-work chain as proof of what happened while they were gone.

bitcoin-org-bitcoin-paper.html — archived snapshot of the bitcoin.org paper page (links to translations and the LaTeX re-typeset editions).

B59-101.001: Whitfield Diffie and Martin E. Hellman · IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, IT-22(6) · November 1976
"We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography."

Before this paper, every cryptographic system rested on a shared secret key that had to be delivered in advance by some trusted channel: a courier, registered mail, a face to face meeting. Diffie and Hellman argued that computer networks made that model untenable, and then showed a way out. Two people with no prior contact could hold a public conversation and end it sharing a secret that a listener to every word could not reconstruct.

The paper defines public key cryptosystems (distinct enciphering and deciphering keys, with the deciphering key infeasible to compute from the enciphering key), public key distribution, and one-way authentication that yields a signature anyone can verify but no one can forge. It gives a concrete key exchange based on exponentiation modulo a prime, the construction now called Diffie-Hellman, and it frames the search for trap-door one-way functions as the central open problem.

Rivest, Shamir and Adleman answered the open problem two years later with RSA. Merkle’s puzzles, developed independently at Berkeley, are the other root of the same tree. Every later system for key agreement, digital signatures, certificate authorities and secure messaging descends from the framework set out here.

Two kinds of contemporary developments in cryptography are examined. Widening applications of teleprocessing have given rise to a need for new types of cryptographic systems, which minimize the need for secure key distribution channels and supply the equivalent of a written signature. This paper suggests ways to solve these currently open problems. It also discusses how the theories of communication and computation are beginning to provide the tools to solve cryptographic problems of long standing.
SOURCE: Whitfield Diffie and Martin E. Hellman, "New Directions in Cryptography," IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, vol. IT-22, no. 6, November 1976, pp. 644-654.

B59-101.002: A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems
R. L. Rivest, A. Shamir, L. Adleman · Communications of the ACM, 21(2) · February 1978
"Publicly revealing an encryption key does not thereby reveal the corresponding decryption key."

Diffie and Hellman described what a public-key system would need to be; RSA is the first one that fully delivered it. Encryption and signatures from a single operation, security reducible to a problem (factoring) that had been studied for centuries, and simple enough to implement on the hardware of the day.

Pick two large primes, publish their product n and an exponent e, keep the primes secret. Encrypting is raising a message to the power e mod n; decrypting is raising to a secret power d recovered from the primes. Signing runs the same math in the other order. Recovering d without the primes appears to require factoring n.

RSA underlies decades of TLS, PGP and GPG, SSH, code signing, and smart-card identity. The cypherpunks built on it directly: PGP is an RSA application, and Chaum’s digital cash uses RSA signatures with a blinding step (see B59-201.001).

An encryption method is presented with the novel property that publicly revealing an encryption key does not thereby reveal the corresponding decryption key. This has two important consequences: (1) Couriers or other secure means are not needed to transmit keys... (2) A message can be "signed" using a privately held decryption key. Anyone can verify this signature using the corresponding publicly revealed encryption key. Signatures cannot be forged, and a signer cannot later deny the validity of his signature. This has obvious applications in "electronic mail" and "electronic funds transfer" systems.
SOURCE: R. L. Rivest, A. Shamir, and L. Adleman, "A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems," Communications of the ACM, vol. 21, no. 2, February 1978, pp. 120-126.

B59-101.003: Ralph C. Merkle · Communications of the ACM, 21(4) · April 1978
"This paper shows that it is possible to select a key over open communications channels in such a fashion that communications security can be maintained."

Merkle got to the core idea of public key cryptography, key agreement without a prior shared secret, independently of Diffie and Hellman and slightly earlier, but publication delays put his paper in print two years after theirs. "New Directions" itself credits him. This is the other origin of the field.

One party sends a large number of "puzzles," each moderately expensive to solve. The other party picks one at random, solves it, and uses its contents as the shared key, sending back only a public identifier for which puzzle was chosen. An eavesdropper does not know which puzzle was picked and must solve them all on average, so the attacker’s cost scales as the square of the honest cost. It is a quadratic gap, not the exponential gap RSA later gave, but it proved the concept was real.

The referee reports Merkle preserved (see "Publishing a New Idea," B59-101.009) are a case study in how established experts receive an idea with no precedent to cite. One reviewer wrote that the work was "not in the main stream of present cryptography thinking."

According to traditional conceptions of cryptographic security, it is necessary to transmit a key, by secret means, before encrypted messages can be sent securely. This paper shows that it is possible to select a key over open communications channels in such a fashion that communications security can be maintained. A method is described which forces any enemy to expend an amount of work which increases as the square of the work required of the two communicants to select the key. The method provides a logically new kind of protection against the passive eavesdropper.
SOURCE: Ralph C. Merkle, "Secure Communications Over Insecure Channels," Communications of the ACM, vol. 21, no. 4, April 1978, pp. 294-299.

B59-101.004: Martin E. Hellman · IEEE Communications Society Magazine, 16(6) · November 1978
"With a public key cryptosystem, the key used to encipher a message can be made public without compromising the secrecy of a different key needed to decipher that message."

"New Directions" was a research paper in an information-theory journal. This is the version Hellman wrote to explain the same ideas to working engineers, in a communications trade magazine, at the exact moment public key cryptography was moving from a small circle into industry. It is a primary record of how the field first pitched itself.

Hellman walks through the commercial case for encryption (wiretapping, automated traffic analysis, electronic mail), then the two capabilities public key methods add: distributing keys over an open channel, and signing messages so a recipient can prove authorship to a third party. He compares the exponential key exchange, the trapdoor knapsack he and Merkle proposed, and the newly published RSA.

The knapsack system Hellman presents here as a leading candidate was broken by Shamir in 1982. That does not date the article so much as show the period honestly: several trapdoor constructions were in play, and it was not yet obvious which would survive.

Cryptography has been of great importance to the military and diplomatic communities since antiquity but failed, until recently, to attract much commercial attention. Recent commercial interest, by contrast, has been almost explosive due to the rapid computerization of information storage, transmission, and spying.

SOURCE: Martin E. Hellman, "An Overview of Public Key Cryptography," IEEE Communications Society Magazine, vol. 16, no. 6, November 1978, pp. 24-32. (Reprinted in IEEE Communications Magazine, 50th Anniversary issue, May 2002.)

B59-101.005: Ralph C. Merkle · IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy · April 1980
"New cryptographic protocols which take full advantage of the unique properties of public key cryptosystems are now evolving."

This is where the hash tree enters the literature. The problem Merkle solves is authenticating one item out of many without signing or storing each one: publish a single root hash, and prove membership with a logarithmic path of hashes. That data structure turned out to matter far beyond cryptographic protocols.

The paper sets the conventional shared-key approach against public key methods for two tasks, distributing keys and signing documents, and weighs the costs of each. It also develops Merkle’s tree-based one-time signature ideas, which he expands in later work.

Merkle trees authenticate the transaction set in every Bitcoin block and the state in most later chains. Certificate Transparency logs, Git commit history, ZFS, BitTorrent and content-addressed storage systems all rest on the same root-and-path idea introduced here.

New cryptographic protocols which take full advantage of the unique properties of public key cryptosystems are now evolving. Several protocols for public key distribution and for digital signatures are briefly compared with each other and with the conventional alternative.

B59-101.006: The First Ten Years of Public-Key Cryptography
Whitfield Diffie · Proceedings of the IEEE, 76(5) · May 1988
Diffie’s own history of the idea he and Hellman set loose, written from inside it, a decade on.

This is the account of public key cryptography’s first decade written by the person best placed to write it. It is the source most later histories lean on for the sequence of events between 1974 and 1984, and for Diffie’s own framing of what the invention did and did not settle.

Diffie separates the concept (splitting the ability to encrypt from the ability to decrypt) from the specific systems that implement it, and shows how fragile the early systems were: several knapsack proposals had already fallen by 1988. He treats digital signatures and protocol design as the parts of the problem still wide open, which is roughly where the cypherpunks picked the thread up.

The paper is careful about attribution, giving Merkle’s puzzle work its due as an independent origin and discussing the claims that would later be confirmed about parallel classified work at GCHQ. It set the tone for how the field talks about its own history.

The archived primary source is a scanned image of the printed article. No verified machine-readable text was available in the archiving environment, so no passage is transcribed here. The complete scan (18 pages) is preserved as the source snapshot linked below; consult it directly for Diffie’s wording.

B59-101.009: Ralph C. Merkle · essay, ralphmerkle.com/1974/ · c. 2005
"The human mind treats a new idea the same way the body treats a strange protein; it rejects it." (P. B. Medawar, quoted by Merkle)

The invention of public key cryptography is usually told through the 1976 Diffie-Hellman paper. This essay is the other half: the record of the same idea being rejected, by a course instructor and then repeatedly by a journal, precisely because it was too original to have citations. Merkle kept the paperwork and published it.

The page links scans of the original 7-page CS244 proposal from Fall 1974, the 2-page simplified resubmission with Hoffman’s handwritten comments, the CACM rejection letter, and a December 1975 revision. It is a complete paper trail of an idea’s first two years.

Merkle explains that he refused to resubmit elsewhere because CACM would have to date any eventual publication to his original 1975 submission, and moving would forfeit that priority. The paper appeared in 1978, after Diffie and Hellman’s, but with its 1975 provenance intact.

In the Fall of 1974, as an undergraduate, I enrolled in CS244, the Computer Security course offered at UC Berkeley and taught by Lance Hoffman. We were required to submit two project proposals, one of which we would complete for the course. I submitted a proposal for what would eventually become known as Public Key Cryptography -- which Hoffman rejected. I dropped the course, but kept working on the idea.

[On the first CACM referee report:] "I am sorry to have to inform you that the paper is not in the main stream of present cryptography thinking and I would not recommend that it be published in the Communications of the ACM." "Experience shows that it is extremely dangerous to transmit key information in the clear."

The more a new idea is unrelated to any prior idea or concept the more it must appear as a squawling bastard, naked and alone, appearing de novo and lacking any respectable pedigree or family to vouch for its acceptability.
SOURCE: Ralph C. Merkle, "Publishing a New Idea," essay, ralphmerkle.com/1974/ (undated; internal references date composition to 2005 or later).

B59-102.001: Ronald L. Rivest · Network Working Group, RFC 1321 · April 1992
"The algorithm takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit fingerprint or message digest of the input."

Cryptographic hash functions are the workhorse primitive of everything the cypherpunks built next: proof-of-work, hash chains, Merkle trees, commitment schemes, content addressing. MD5 was, through the 1990s and 2000s, the default one. This RFC is how it was specified and spread.

A padding rule, a 128-bit state, and four rounds of 16 operations mixing the message into that state, plus a full reference implementation in C. The "conservative" design note explains that MD5 deliberately traded some of MD4’s speed for a wider security margin.

Collisions in MD5 were demonstrated in 2004 and made cheap thereafter, and it must not be used where collision resistance matters (certificates, signatures). It survives as a fast non-security checksum and as a case study in how hash functions fail. The RFC is kept here as the historical record, not as a recommendation.

This document describes the MD5 message-digest algorithm. The algorithm takes as input a message of arbitrary length and produces as output a 128-bit "fingerprint" or "message digest" of the input. It is conjectured that it is computationally infeasible to produce two messages having the same message digest, or to produce any message having a given prespecified target message digest. The MD5 algorithm is intended for digital signature applications, where a large file must be "compressed" in a secure manner before being encrypted with a private (secret) key under a public-key cryptosystem such as RSA. ... The MD5 algorithm is being placed in the public domain for review and possible adoption as a standard.
SOURCE: R. Rivest, "The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm," RFC 1321, Internet Engineering Task Force, April 1992.

B59-103.001: Ralph C. Merkle · written 1979, published in Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO ’89
"A digital signature based only on a conventional encryption function... as secure as the underlying encryption function."

This paper shows you can build a general-purpose digital signature from a hash function alone, with no number theory, no factoring, no discrete logs. That makes the scheme immune to the quantum attacks that threaten RSA and elliptic-curve signatures, which is why hash-based signatures are back in the NIST post-quantum standards (SPHINCS+, XMSS, LMS) that trace directly to this construction.

A one-time signature (Lamport style) lets you sign a single message by revealing pre-images of a hash. Merkle’s tree turns many one-time keys into one reusable public key: the root hash certifies every leaf, and each signature carries the authentication path proving its leaf belongs. The result signs an effectively unlimited number of messages, with signature size growing only logarithmically.

B59-201.001: David Chaum · Advances in Cryptology, Proceedings of CRYPTO ’82 · Santa Barbara, August 1982
A signature you can obtain on a message without the signer seeing the message, the cryptographic core of anonymous digital cash.

Chaum’s mix networks (B59-303.001) anonymized communication. This paper anonymizes money. It is the first construction that lets a bank issue currency it cannot trace, and it defined the problem, payer anonymity with issuer control and double-spend detection, that digital cash has worked on ever since.

The user multiplies the coin value by a random blinding factor before sending it to the bank. The bank signs the blinded value (debiting the account) and returns it. The user divides out the blinding factor, leaving a genuine bank signature on the original coin. The bank has never seen that coin and cannot recognize it at deposit, but the signature is valid and unforgeable.

Chaum founded DigiCash in 1989 to commercialize this; its ecash system ran trials with several banks before the company failed in 1998 (see B59-001.005). The idea outlived the company: Chaumian ecash is being actively rebuilt today in Bitcoin mints such as Cashu and Fedimint.

The archived primary source is a scanned image of the printed paper (CRYPTO ’82 proceedings, pp. 199-203). No verified machine-readable text was available in the archiving environment, so no passage is transcribed here. Consult the source snapshot linked below for Chaum’s wording.

B59-203.001: Security without Identification: Card Computers to Make Big Brother Obsolete
David Chaum · Communications of the ACM, 28(10) · October 1985
"Computerization is robbing individuals of the ability to monitor and control the ways information about them is used."

This is the fullest statement of the idea the cypherpunks organized around: that the privacy properties of the systems being automated in the 1980s were being fixed by default, invisibly, and that cryptography offered a genuine alternative if adopted before the identity-based version set. Eric Hughes’ 1993 "A Cypherpunk’s Manifesto" (B59-302.004) is a compression of this argument.

Individuals interact with organizations under different unlinkable pseudonyms, transfer credentials between those pseudonyms without making them linkable, and pay with the untraceable cash of the blind-signature scheme (B59-201.001). Organizations still get authenticated transactions and fraud control; they just do not get a cross-linkable dossier.

The "card computer" is a smartphone. The "mass surveillance from everyday consumer transactions" is the ad-tech and data-broker economy. Chaum described both, and an alternative, in 1985. Which parts were technically necessary and which were choices is the live question the paper still forces.

Computerization is robbing individuals of the ability to monitor and control the ways information about them is used. ... New and more serious dangers derive from computerized pattern recognition techniques: even a small group using these and tapping into data gathered in everyday consumer transactions could secretly conduct mass surveillance, inferring individuals’ lifestyles, activities, and associations. ... This conflict may be avoided by early adoption of a fundamentally different approach to automating transaction systems.

B59-204.001: B59-204.001 · WRITING · DIGITAL CASH · B-MONEY
Wei Dai · cypherpunks mailing list, 1998 · weidai.com/bmoney.txt
A scheme for a group of untraceable digital pseudonyms to pay each other with money and to enforce contracts amongst themselves without outside help.

b-money opens by taking Tim May’s crypto-anarchy as its premise and asking the practical question: how would such a community actually transact? Its answer needs a medium of exchange and a way to enforce contracts, provided to and by untraceable entities.

Dai gives two protocols. In the first, every participant maintains a copy of the ledger; money is created by broadcasting the solution to "a previously unsolved computational problem," with the amount minted equal to the cost of the computation in a standard basket of commodities — proof-of-work as issuance. Contracts are entered by all parties (and an arbitrator) posting bonded signatures, with disputes settled by each participant computing a fine schedule. The second protocol delegates the ledger to a set of servers who must post bonds and periodically publish their databases.
Satoshi cited b-money as reference [1] of the Bitcoin white paper; Adam Back has said he pointed Satoshi to Dai’s page after Satoshi emailed him about hashcash (see B59-400.005).

B59-204.003: Preserved by Project B59 · ← Return to The Vault

A long time ago I hit upon the idea of bit gold. The problem, in a nutshell, is that our money currently depends on trust in a third party for its value. As many inflationary and hyperinflationary episodes during the 20th century demonstrated, this is not an ideal state of affairs. Similarly, private bank note issue , while it had various advantages as well as disadvantages, similarly depended on a trusted third party.

Precious metals and collectibles have an unforgeable scarcity due to the costliness of their creation. This once provided money the value of which was largely independent of any trusted third party. Precious metals have problems, however. It’s too costly to assay metals repeatedly for common transactions. Thus a trusted third party (usually associated with a tax collector who accepted the coins as payment) was invoked to stamp a standard amount of the metal into a coin. Transporting large values of metal can be a rather insecure affair, as the British found when transporting gold across a U-boat infested Atlantic to Canada during World War I to support their gold standard. What’s worse, you can’t pay online with metal.

Thus, it would be very nice if there were a protocol whereby unforgeably costly bits could be created online with minimal dependence on trusted third parties, and then securely stored, transferred, and assayed with similar minimal trust. Bit gold.

My proposal for bit gold is based on computing a string of bits from a string of challenge bits, using functions called variously “client puzzle function,” “proof of work function,” or “secure benchmark function.” The resulting string of bits is the proof of work. Where a one-way function is prohibitively difficult to compute backwards, a secure benchmark function ideally comes with a specific cost, measured in compute cycles, to compute backwards.
Here are the main steps of the bit gold system that I envision:
A public string of bits, the “challenge string,” is created (see step 5).
Alice on her computer generates the proof of work string from the challenge bits using a benchmark function.

The proof of work is securely timestamped . This should work in a distributed fashion, with several different timestamp services so that no particular timestamp service need be substantially relied on.

Alice adds the challenge string and the timestamped proof of work string to a distributed property title registry for bit gold. Here, too, no single server is substantially relied on to properly operate the registry.
B59-204.004: Preserved by Project B59 · ← Return to The Vault

The basic idea of bit gold is for “bit gold miners” to set their computers to solving computationally intensive mathematical puzzles, then to publish the solutions to these puzzles in secure public registries, giving them unique title to these provably scarce and securely timestamped bits. These titles to timestamped bits will be more secure and provably scarce than precious metals, collectibles, and any other objects that have ever been used as money. In a description of bit gold, which was mostly an overview of the technology, I wrote about how, because the algorithms and architectures for solving computationally intensive mathematical puzzles to create bit gold will often be dramatically improved, the bits (the puzzle solutions) from one period (anywhere from seconds to weeks, let’s say a week) to the next are not fungible. But fungible units can be created from non-fungible ones:

bit gold will not be fungible based on a simple function of, for example, the length of the string. Instead, to create fungible units dealers will have to combine different-valued pieces of bit gold into larger units of approximately equal value. This is analogous to what many commodity dealers do today [pooling commodities with a wide variety of qualities into a handful of standard grades] to make commodity markets possible.

Bit strings (puzzle problem/solution pairs) are securely timestamped by their time of publication. More recent solutions that have been produced in greater quantities will be discounted by markets. To create fungible units dealers will bundle strings of different value into pools of a standard value (i.e. collect strings into a pool so that the sum of the market values of the strings in the pool add up to the standard value).

It’s a bit indirect, but computers can easily handle these logistics. Leaving aside the gold metaphor for a minute, one can think of these bit strings as digital rare postage stamps. Each stamp might trade for a different price, but one can sort stamps into pools so that the prices of stamps in each pool add up to the same total price. Then divide each pool into tranches to create your standard currency denominations.

B59-205.001: PayWord and MicroMint: Two Simple Micropayment Schemes
Ronald L. Rivest and Adi Shamir · Security Protocols Workshop, Cambridge · April 1996
"Our main goal is to minimize the number of public-key operations required per payment, using hash operations instead whenever possible."

The micropayment problem, how to charge a fraction of a cent without spending more than that in processing, drove a decade of pre-Bitcoin digital-cash design. PayWord’s answer, amortize one signature over a chain of cheap hashes, is the same trick that reappears in probabilistic payments (B59-205.002) and later in Lightning-style payment channels.

PayWord: the user commits to the end of a hash chain with a single signed message, then releases pre-images one at a time as payment; the vendor redeems only the last one it received. MicroMint: coins are k-way hash collisions, whose cost per coin drops sharply at scale, so only a large broker can mint them economically.
Hash chains as payment appear again in Rivest’s lottery-ticket scheme, in NetBill and Millicent-era systems, and structurally in the HTLC and channel-update mechanics of the Lightning Network.

We present two simple micropayment schemes, "PayWord" and "MicroMint," for making small purchases over the Internet. ... Our main goal is to minimize the number of public-key operations required per payment, using hash operations instead whenever possible. As a rough guide, hash functions are about 100 times faster than RSA signature verification, and about 10,000 times faster than RSA signature generation.

B59-205.002: Ronald L. Rivest · Financial Cryptography ’97, Anguilla · February 1997
"This scheme is exceptionally efficient since the bank handles only winning tickets, instead of handling each micropayment."

It reframes efficiency: you cannot make processing a one-cent payment cost less than a cent, but you can make most one-cent payments generate no processing at all. Expected value stays honest; variance does the work. This is the conceptual seed of "don’t settle every payment on the ledger."

A payment is a signed ticket that is valid only if some later-revealed value hashes into a winning range. The vendor accepts many losing tickets knowing the winners, scaled up in value, average out to what it is owed. Only winners are ever sent to the bank.

Probabilistic and aggregated payments run through MICROPAYMENTS research into Peppercoin (Rivest and Micali), and the "bank sees only net results" principle is exactly what payment channels and rollups generalize.

We present a new micropayment scheme based on the use of "electronic lottery tickets." This scheme is exceptionally efficient since the bank handles only winning tickets, instead of handling each micropayment.

We present intuitive arguments for why micropayments have not succeeded on the Internet. The “hassle factor” for customers asso ciated with such transactions is characterized. A framework of mental transaction costs and price granularity is then presented, and arguments ab out micropayments recast in its light. Finally, we make some suggestions for reducing the mental transaction costs of Internet commerce.

Some Internet payment system pro jects promise dramatically lower transaction costs, so that we can achieve micropayments (e.g. [Be95] , [GMAGS95] , [RS96] ). Other projects propose more sophisticated forms of microtransaction [MD88] . To what extent can transction costs be reduced in these ways? This paper will argue that mental transaction costs raise fundamental barriers to customer acceptance of fine grained bundling and pricing. We will explore the problems both informally and through a closer examination of three sources of customer cognitive expenditures.

These mental accounting costs, not the physical or computation or amortized R&D costs of a payment or billing method, set the main lower bound on price granularity. Judging from price granularity is far above suggested micropayment levels of a few cents or even fractions of a cent. The mental accounting costs for a typical on-line consumer seem to be somewhat higher than those in more familiar areas of commerce.
Customer mental transaction costs come from at least three sources: uncertain cashflors, incomplete and costly observation of product attributes, and incomplete and costly decision making.

For electronic commerce economics, it’s important to distinguish between technological and mental transaction costs. When technologists talk about transaction costs, they are usually talking about computation and network costs. Thus the claim that micropayment technologies, which dramatically reduce these costs, will reduce “transaction costs.” The significance of such technological reductions depends on the accompanying cognitive costs already being very low, since these payments don’t address cognitive costs.
B59-301.003: Frequently Asked Questions About the EFF DES Cracker
EFF’s DES Cracker entered and won the RSA DES Challenge II-2 competition in less than 3 days, proving that DES is not secure and that such a machine is inexpensive to design and build.
The FAQ is the companion piece to the "Cracking DES" book (B59-301.002): where the book gives the full engineering detail, this document is the version written for reporters and policymakers.

Its throughline is credibility. The EFF lays the government’s past statements about DES next to what a quarter-million-dollar machine actually did, and asks why officials had been allowed to make unverifiable claims about a standard that banks, and much of the internet, depended on.

The last questions turn to export policy: the FAQ argues that the controls treating cryptography as a munition had suppressed exactly the open research that would have shown DES was too weak, and points readers to the Bernstein litigation then working through the courts.

B59-302.001: Timothy C. May · written mid-1988, first read at the founding Cypherpunks meeting, September 1992
A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.

Written in 1988 and read aloud at the founding meeting of the Cypherpunks in September 1992, this is the document that gave the movement its name and its founding claim: that strong cryptography would let people transact, communicate, and organize without revealing who they are, and that no government could stop it.

May wrote it four years before PGP was in wide use and sixteen years before Bitcoin. The specific technologies he names (ISDN, smart cards, Ku-band transmitters) mostly didn’t become the enabling layer he expected. The argument underneath them did: that public-key cryptography changes the balance of power between individuals and the state by making certain kinds of surveillance and control structurally impossible, not just illegal.
The closing line borrows the closing line of the Communist Manifesto on purpose. May meant crypto anarchy as a rival revolution, driven by mathematics instead of by seizing the means of production.
A specter is haunting the modern world, the specter of crypto anarchy.

Computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner. Two persons may exchange messages, conduct business, and negotiate electronic contracts without ever knowing the True Name, or legal identity, of the other. Interactions over networks will be untraceable, via extensive re- routing of encrypted packets and tamper-proof boxes which implement cryptographic protocols with nearly perfect assurance against any tampering. Reputations will be of central importance, far more important in dealings than even the credit ratings of today. These developments will alter completely the nature of government regulation, the ability to tax and control economic interactions, the ability to keep information secret, and will even alter the nature of trust and reputation.
B59-302.002: St. Jude and the Origin of the Word "Cypherpunk"
You guys are just a bunch of cypherpunks.

Jude Milhon is the reason the movement has the name it has. She was not primarily a cryptographer; she was a programmer and writer who had been online since the early 1970s, first on the Berkeley Computer Company system and then on Community Memory, the public terminal network she helped build in a Berkeley record shop.

By 1992 she was a senior editor at Mondo 2000, the Bay Area magazine that covered the collision of psychedelia, hacking and early virtual reality. When Eric Hughes, Tim May and John Gilmore started holding meetings about cryptography and privacy, Milhon was there, and her offhand line, "you guys are just a bunch of cypherpunks," stuck to the group permanently.

She kept pushing the movement to stay human and to make room for women in it: "Girls need modems" was hers. This record collects what can be documented and sourced about the coinage; it is deliberately small, because most of Milhon’s own writing remains under copyright and cannot be hosted here.

Tim May, The Cyphernomicon (v0.666, 10 September 1994), §2.4.10, "Where did the name ‘Cypherpunks’ come from?": "Jude Milhon, aka St. Jude, then an editor at ‘Mondo 2000,’ was at the earliest meetings … she quipped ‘You guys are just a bunch of cypherpunks.’ The name was adopted immediately." (Quoted here under the FAQ’s own fair-use terms, with attribution.)

B59-302.004: Where Tim May’s manifesto argues from consequences, Eric Hughes’ argues from first principles: what privacy actually is, why it requires cryptography rather than trust, and why cypherpunks build rather than lobby.

The distinction Hughes opens with, privacy is not secrecy, became one of the most cited framings in the field: a private matter is something you don’t want the whole world to know, a secret matter is something you don’t want anybody to know. Privacy is the power to selectively reveal yourself, not the absence of disclosure.

The line “Cypherpunks write code” became the movement’s working method as much as its slogan: PGP, remailers, and later Bitcoin all came out of people who took that sentence literally rather than treating privacy as a policy problem to be argued about.

Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age. Privacy is not secrecy. A private matter is something one doesn't want the whole world to know, but a secret matter is something one doesn't want anybody to know. Privacy is the power to selectively reveal oneself to the world.

If two parties have some sort of dealings, then each has a memory of their interaction. Each party can speak about their own memory of this; how could anyone prevent it? One could pass laws against it, but the freedom of speech, even more than privacy, is fundamental to an open society; we seek not to restrict any speech at all. If many parties speak together in the same forum, each can speak to all the others and aggregate together knowledge about individuals and other parties. The power of electronic communications has enabled such group speech, and it will not go away merely because we might want it to.

Since we desire privacy, we must ensure that each party to a transaction have knowledge only of that which is directly necessary for that transaction. Since any information can be spoken of, we must ensure that we reveal as little as possible. In most cases personal identity is not salient. When I purchase a magazine at a store and hand cash to the clerk, there is no need to know who I am. When I ask my electronic mail provider to send and receive messages, my provider need not know to whom I am speaking or what I am saying or what others are saying to me; my provider only need know how to get the message there and how much I owe them in fees. When my identity is revealed by the underlying mechanism of the transaction, I have no privacy. I cannot here selectively reveal myself; I must always reveal myself.

B59-302.008: The Cypherpunks have existed since September, 1992. In that time, a vast amount has been written on cryptography, key escrow, Clipper, the Net, cyber terrorists, and crypto anarchy.

The Cyphernomicon is the nearest thing the cypherpunks produced to a canonical text. May began it as a mailing-list FAQ and let it grow until it covered nearly everything the group had argued about in its first two years: why strong cryptography changes the balance of power between individuals and states, how remailers and digital cash and reputations would actually work, and what the movement expected the government to do about it.

It is deliberately unedited. May kept contradictions, false starts, and his own asides in place rather than smoothing them out, on the view that an honest record of an argument in progress was more useful than a polished summary. The result is long, uneven, and often the only surviving account of a given early idea.

The title borrows H.P. Lovecraft's fictional Necronomicon. May released it, he said, before the RSA patents ran out, so that the ideas would be in wide circulation before the tools became unencumbered.

B59-303.001: Untraceable Electronic Mail, Return Addresses, and Digital Pseudonyms
David L. Chaum · Communications of the ACM, 24(2) · February 1981
"A technique... that allows an electronic mail system to hide who a participant communicates with as well as the content of the communication."

Encryption hides message content; it does nothing about the pattern of who contacts whom. Chaum was the first to treat that metadata as the harder problem and to give a construction that beats it without a trusted party. The cypherpunk remailer culture is a direct application of this paper.

Wrap a message in nested public-key encryption, one layer per mix. Each mix strips its layer, holds messages until it has a batch, shuffles them, and forwards. An observer sees a message go into the first mix and a different-looking message come out, with no way to match them. Return addresses work the same way in reverse. Anonymity holds as long as at least one mix in the path is honest.

Type I (cypherpunk) and Type II (Mixmaster) remailers, Mixminion, onion routing, and Tor are all mix-network designs. Digital pseudonyms, the idea of a persistent unlinkable identity you control, run from here through Chaum’s credential work (B59-203.001) into modern anonymous-credential systems.

A technique based on public key cryptography is presented that allows an electronic mail system to hide who a participant communicates with as well as the content of the communication -- in spite of an unsecured underlying telecommunication system. The technique does not require a universally trusted authority. One correspondent can remain anonymous to a second, while allowing the second to respond via an untraceable return address. The technique can also be used to form rosters of untraceable digital pseudonyms from selected applications.
SOURCE: David L. Chaum, "Untraceable Electronic Mail, Return Addresses, and Digital Pseudonyms," Communications of the ACM, vol. 24, no. 2, February 1981, pp. 84-88.

B59-303.015: B59-303.015 · WRITING · ANONYMITY · PIPENET
Wei Dai · cypherpunks mailing list, c. 1998 · weidai.com/pipenet.txt
Constant-rate, constant-size packet streams: buy traffic-analysis resistance by refusing to let timing carry information.

PipeNet is the other half of Wei Dai’s late-1990s cypherpunks work, developed in the same window as b-money. Where later systems optimise for usability, PipeNet optimises for the hardest version of the anonymity property.

Every link carries a fixed-rate stream of constant-size packets whether or not there is traffic to send. Each switch holds a key, a hop id and two link ids; per time unit it expects exactly one packet per link id, decrypts it, checks its sequence number and MAC, re-randomises them, re-tags the packet for the next link and forwards packets in shuffled order. The cost is bandwidth and a deliberate global failure mode: if one packet is late, the network stalls rather than leak timing.

PipeNet is routinely cited in the lineage that runs through mix networks to onion routing and Tor; Adam Back’s ZKS "Freedom network" work and Wei Dai’s attacks on it are part of the same conversation.
Consider a network of processors which send messages to each other
asynchronously. We assume that each node is identified by its public key,
and that links between nodes are secure. The adversary may control a
fixed subset of the nodes. All messages between any two honest
nodes are confidential and always arrive (unmodified) in the order sent
(this can be achieved with a standard transport level security protocol),
but the adversary may delay any message by an arbitrary time interval.
The protocol is based on the idea of virtual link encryption.
After an anonymous connection is established, the originating node sends a
constant stream of (constant size) packets to a second node at a fixed
rate. The second node shuffles the packets it receives during a time unit
and forwards them in random order to others.
A connection is a path in the network. The first node in the path is the
caller, and the last node is the receiver. The rest are called switches.
Anonymity in this scheme is asymmetric - the caller is anonymous, but not
the receiver. Each node in the path shares a key with the caller and
knows the nodes immediately in front of and behind it. Each node also
knows its hop id (how many hops away it is from the caller). Every pair
Each switch in a path therefore has a key, an associated hop id, and two
associated link ids. Call the id that it shares with the previous node
(the one closer to the caller) type A, and call the other link id type B.

Mixminion: Design of a Type III Anonymous Remailer Protocol
Nick Mathewson The Free Haven Project nickm@freehaven.net

We present Mixminion, a message-based anonymous remailer protocol with secure single-use reply blocks. Mix nodes cannot distinguish Mixminion forward messages from reply messages, so forward and reply messages share the same anonymity set. We add directory servers that allow users to learn public keys and performance statistics of participating remailers, and we describe nymservers that provide long-term pseudonyms using single-use reply blocks as a primitive. Our design integrates link encryption between remailers to provide forward anonymity. Mixminion works in a real-world Internet environment, requires little synchronization or coordination between nodes, and protects against known anonymity-breaking attacks as well as or better than other systems with similar design parameters.

Chaum first introduced anonymous remailers over 20 years ago [7]. The research community has since introduced many new designs and proofs [1, 14, 16, 19, 28, 29], and discovered a variety of new attacks [3, 5, 6, 9, 23, 35]. But because many of the newer designs require considerable coordination, synchronization, bandwidth, or processing resources, deployed remailers still use Cottrell's Mixmaster design from 1994 [8, 26]. Here we describe Mixminion, a protocol for asynchronous, loosely federated remailers that maintains Mixmaster's flexibility while addressing the following flaws:

� Replies: Mixmaster does not support replies or anonymous recipients -- people who want these functions must use the older and less secure Cypherpunk Type I remailer design [31], which is vulnerable to replay attacks. We introduce a new primitive called a singleuse reply block (SURB), which makes replies as secure as forward messages. Furthermore in Mixminion the remailers themselves cannot distinguish reply messages from forward messages. We also describe how
to use these SURBs to securely build higher-level systems such as nymservers. By integrating reply capabilities into Mixminion, we can finally retire the Type I remailer network.

B59-304.001: It's personal. It's private. And it's no one's business but yours.

This essay began life in 1991 as the section of the first PGP User’s Guide titled "Why Do You Need PGP?" Zimmermann rewrote and extended it through the 1990s; the version archived here is the 1999 revision from his own website.

The argument is deliberately not technical. Zimmermann puts privacy on the same footing as the privacy of a sealed letter or a face-to-face conversation: something that was simply assumed until electronic communication made interception cheap and invisible. If only people with something to hide encrypt, he notes, then encrypting marks you out; privacy has to be normal to protect anyone.

The 1999 material adds the point Zimmermann is now best known for: technology infrastructures persist for generations, so a surveillance capability built today under a benign government will still be there when a less benign one takes office. "If we do nothing, new technologies will give the government new automatic surveillance capabilities that Stalin could never have dreamed of."
Part of the Original 1991 PGP User's Guide (updated in 1999)
"Whatever you do will be insignificant, but it is very important that you do it." -Mahatma Gandhi

It's personal. It's private. And it's no one's business but yours. You may be planning a political campaign, discussing your taxes, or having an illicit affair. Or you may be communicating with a political dissident in a repressive country. Whatever it is, you don't want your private electronic mail (email) or confidential documents read by anyone else. There's nothing wrong with asserting your privacy. Privacy is as apple-pie as the Constitution.

The right to privacy is spread implicitly throughout the Bill of Rights. But when the United States Constitution was framed, the Founding Fathers saw no need to explicitly spell out the right to a private conversation. That would have been silly. Two hundred years ago, all conversations were private. If someone else was within earshot, you could just go out behind the barn and have your conversation there. No one could listen in without your knowledge. The right to a private conversation was a natural right, not just in a philosophical sense, but in a law-of-physics sense, given the technology of the time.

B59-304.003: Testimony of Philip R. Zimmermann to the US Senate Subcommittee on Science, Technology, and Space
Philip Zimmermann · 26 June 1996 · US Senate, Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
If we do nothing, new technologies will give the government new automatic surveillance capabilities that Stalin could never have dreamed of.

By mid-1996 the crypto wars were turning. The Customs Service investigation of Zimmermann had just been dropped; the Clipper chip proposal had stalled; and bills in both houses of Congress were proposing to loosen the export rules that treated strong encryption as a munition. Zimmermann testified for one of them, the Pro-CODE bill.

His argument is practical as much as principled: the export regime had not kept PGP or any other serious cryptography out of foreign hands, but it had pushed development overseas and left Americans using deliberately weakened products. Meanwhile the digital telephony law (CALEA) was building wiretap capacity directly into the phone network.

The closing passage is the one still quoted: infrastructures outlast the governments that build them, so a system designed for mass surveillance under a trusted administration becomes a standing danger under any future one.
Testimony of Philip R. Zimmermann to the Subcommittee on Science, Technology, and Space of the US Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

I'm here to talk to you today about S.1726 and the need to change US export control policy for cryptographic software. I want to thank you for the opportunity to be here to speak in favor of this bill.

I'm the creator of PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), a public-key encryption software package for the protection of electronic mail. B59-304.004: It was on this day in 1991 that I sent the first release of PGP to a couple of my friends for uploading to the Internet.

There is no single contemporaneous "release announcement" for PGP 1.0; it went out in June 1991 as a quiet upload by two friends. This 2001 essay is Zimmermann’s own reconstruction of those days and is the most detailed first-hand account of the release sequence.

The "US only" detail matters historically: Zimmermann believed the Usenet tag would keep the posting inside the country. It did not, and the program’s appearance on foreign servers is what triggered the export investigation. He is candid that in 1991 he barely understood how newsgroups propagated.

The essay also dates the tools of the movement: PGP 2.0 in September 1992, built by volunteers around the world, with the trust model Zimmermann had not had time to finish for 1.0. That trust model is documented in B59-304.002.
Today marks the 10th anniversary of the release of PGP 1.0.

It was on this day in 1991 that I sent the first release of PGP to a couple of my friends for uploading to the Internet. First, I sent it to Allan Hoeltje, who posted it to Peacenet, an ISP that specialized in grassroots political organizations, mainly in the peace movement. Peacenet was accessible to political activists all over the world. Then, I uploaded it to Kelly Goen, who proceeded to upload it to a Usenet newsgroup that specialized in distributing source code. At my request, he marked the Usenet posting as "US only". Kelly also uploaded it to many BBS systems around the country. I don't recall if the postings to the Internet began on June 5th or 6th.

It may be surprising to some that back in 1991, I did not yet know enough about Usenet newsgroups to realize that a "US only" tag was merely an advisory tag that had little real effect on how Usenet propagated newsgroup postings. I thought it actually controlled how Usenet routed the posting. But back then, I had no clue how to post anything on a newsgroup, and didn't even have a clear idea what a newsgroup was.

B59-305.002: Bernstein v. United States (EFF case archive)
Code is speech. In 1996 a graduate student named Daniel Bernstein sued the US government for the right to publish a cryptographic algorithm.

While a graduate student at the University of California at Berkeley, Bernstein completed the development of an encryption equation (an "algorithm") he calls "Snuffle." Bernstein wishes to publish a) the algorithm (b) a mathematical paper describing and explaining the algorithm and (c) the "source code" for a computer program that incorporates the algorithm. Bernstein also wishes to discuss these items at mathematical conferences, college classrooms and other open public meetings. The Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (the ITAR regulatory scheme) required Bernstein to submit his ideas about cryptography to the government for review, to register as an arms dealer, and to apply for and obtain from the government a license to publish his ideas. Failure to do so would result in severe civil and criminal penalties. Bernstein believes this is a violation of his First Amendment rights and has sued the government.

After four years and one regulatory change, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that software source code was speech protected by the First Amendment and that the government's regulations preventing its publication were unconstitutional.

I look up and there's these two strangers riding into town. They're young and got kind of a restless, bored way about 'em. A person don't need both eyes to see they mean trouble...

Howard: Interesting couple of newusers just signed on. One calls himself acid and the other's optik.
Barlow: Hmmm. What are their real names?
And so I typed !finger acid. Several seconds later the WELL's Sequent computer sent the following message to my Macintosh in Wyoming:

By this, I knew that the WELL had a new resident and that his corporeal analog was supposedly called Acid Phreak. Typing !finger optik yielded results of similar insufficiency, including the claim that someone, somewhere in the real world, was walking around calling himself Phiber Optik. I doubted it.

However, associating these sparse data with the knowledge that the WELL was about to host a conference on computers and security rendered the conclusion that I had made my first sighting of genuine computer crackers. As the arrival of an outlaw was a major event to the settlements of the Old West, so was the appearance of crackers cause for stir on the WELL.

The WELL (or Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link) is an example of the latest thing in frontier villages, the computer bulletin board. In this kind of small town, Main Street is a central minicomputer to which (in the case of the WELL) as many as 64 microcomputers may be connected at one time by phone lines and little blinking boxes called modems.

In this silent world, all conversation is typed. To enter it, one forsakes both body and place and becomes a thing of words alone. You can see what your neighbors are saying (or recently said), but not what either they or their physical surroundings look like. Town meetings are continuous and discussions rage on everything from sexual kinks to depreciation schedules.
B59-306.002: Mitchell Kapor & John Perry Barlow · 10 July 1990

We are founding the Electronic Frontier Foundation to deal with these and related challenges. While our agenda is ambitious to the point of audacity, we don't see that these issues are being given the broad social attention they deserve.
by: Mitchell Kapor and John Perry Barlow

Over the last 50 years, the people of the developed world have begun to cross into a landscape unlike any which humanity has experienced before. It is a region without physical shape or form. It exists, like a standing wave, in the vast web of our electronic communication systems. It consists of electron states, microwaves, magnetic fields, light pulses and thought itself.

It is familiar to most people as the "place" in which a long-distance telephone conversation takes place. But it is also the repository for all digital or electronically transferred information, and, as such, it is the venue for most of what is now commerce, industry, and broad-scale human interaction. William Gibson called this Platonic realm "Cyberspace," a name which has some currency among its present inhabitants.
Whatever it is eventually called, it is the homeland of the Information Age, the place where the future is destined to dwell.

In its present condition, Cyberspace is a frontier region, populated by the few hardy technologists who can tolerate the austerity of its savage computer interfaces, incompatible communications protocols, proprietary barricades, cultural and legal ambiguities, and general lack of useful maps or metaphors.
Certainly, the old concepts of property, expression, identity, movement, and context, based as they are on physical manifestation, do not apply succinctly in a world where there can be none.

Sovereignty over this new world is also not well defined. Large institutions already lay claim to large fiefdoms, but most of the actual natives are solitary and independent, sometimes to the point of sociopathy. It is, therefore, a perfect breeding ground for both outlaws and vigilantes. Most of society has chosen to ignore the existence of this arising domain. Every day millions of people use ATM's and credit cards, place telephone calls, make travel reservations, and access information of limitless variety. . . all without any perception of the digital machinations behind these transactions.

B59-306.006: "The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it"
John Gilmore · quoted in TIME, 6 December 1993 · annotation from toad.com/gnu/
The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it.

The sentence is usually cited as a law of the internet. Gilmore’s own gloss is narrower and more interesting: in its original form it was about the Usenet news software, which passed messages between discussion servers by many redundant paths, so that a server refusing to carry a newsgroup did not stop the articles reaching everyone else.

He also ties it to IP packet routing, which reroutes around broken links and dead routers. He is careful to note what it does not mean: routing protocols do not detect selective censorship, only outright failure of a node.

Over thirty years the phrase outgrew its origin. Gilmore accepts that: if you count the people and institutions who use the network as part of the network, then every time a threatened document is mirrored and reposted, the aphorism is proven again.
From John Gilmore’s home page, "Things I’ve Said (That People Sometimes Remember)"
Things I've Said (That People Sometimes Remember)
"The Net interprets censorship as damage and routes around it."

This was quoted in Time Magazine's December 6, 1993 article "First Nation in Cyberspace", by Philip Elmer-DeWitt. It's been reprinted hundreds or thousands of times since then, including the NY Times on January 15, 1996, Scientific American of October 2000, and CACM 39(7):13.

In its original form, it meant that the Usenet software (which moves messages around in discussion newsgroups) was resistant to censorship because, if a node drops certain messages because it doesn't like their subject, the messages find their way past that node anyway by some other route. This is also a reference to the packet-routing protocols that the Internet uses to direct packets around any broken wires or fiber connections or routers. (They don't redirect around selective censorship, but they do recover if an entire node is shut down to censor it.)

The meaning of the phrase has grown through the years. Internet users have proven it time after time, by personally and publicly replicating information that is threatened with destruction or censorship. If you now consider the Net to be not only the wires and machines, but the people and their social structures who use the machines, it is more true than ever.

Bitcoin open source implementation of P2P currency
Satoshi Nakamoto · P2P Foundation forum · 11 February 2009
The root problem with conventional currency is all the trust that’s required to make it work.

On 11 February 2009 Satoshi announced Bitcoin a second time, now to a general audience, on Ning's P2P Foundation forum. Where the metzdowd post was a cryptographer talking to cryptographers, this one states the motivation in plain terms: the problem Bitcoin exists to solve is trust .

The analogy it draws — that strong encryption once removed the need to trust a system administrator with your files, and cryptographic money can now do the same for your money — is the clearest short statement of the cypherpunk logic behind the project. It is reproduced here in full; these are Satoshi's words only.

The root problem with conventional currency is all the trust that's required to make it work. The central bank must be trusted not to debase the currency, but the history of fiat currencies is full of breaches of that trust. Banks must be trusted to hold our money and transfer it electronically, but they lend it out in waves of credit bubbles with barely a fraction in reserve. We have to trust them with our privacy, trust them not to let identity thieves drain our accounts. Their massive overhead costs make micropayments impossible.

A generation ago, multi-user time-sharing computer systems had a similar problem. Before strong encryption, users had to rely on password protection to secure their files, placing trust in the system administrator to keep their information private. Privacy could always be overridden by the admin based on his judgment call weighing the principle of privacy against other concerns, or at the behest of his superiors. Then strong encryption became available to the masses, and trust was no longer required. Data could be secured in a way that was physically impossible for others to access, no matter for what reason, no matter how good the excuse, no matter what.
It's time we had the same thing for money. With e-currency based on cryptographic proof, without the need to trust a third party middleman, money can be secure and transactions effortless.

B59-401.001: Stuart Haber & W. Scott Stornetta · Bellcore · Journal of Cryptology, 1991
Hash each new record together with the one before it, and the sequence becomes something no one can quietly rewrite.
This is where the block chain’s core trick comes from. Haber and Stornetta pose the problem of proving when a digital document existed, without having to trust whoever runs the timestamping service.

Their first mechanism is linking: the timestamp certificate for each document includes the hash of the previous certificate, so the certificates form a chain — altering one record means redoing every record after it. Their second is distributed trust: the document’s own hash pseudorandomly selects several independent parties who must each co-sign the timestamp, so no single party can backdate or forge.

The Bitcoin white paper cites this work; Satoshi’s "The network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work" is this paper’s linking scheme with proof-of-work added. The full PDF is attached.

B59-401.002: Improving the Efficiency and Reliability of Digital Time-Stamping
Dave Bayer, Stuart Haber & W. Scott Stornetta · 1993
Combine an interval’s documents into a hash tree; one root value witnesses them all, and each proof is just the path to the root.

Two years after "How to Time-Stamp a Digital Document," the same authors — now with mathematician Dave Bayer — make the scheme practical. Instead of a single linked list of certificates, the documents submitted in each time period are combined with a Merkle hash tree.

That gives two things Bitcoin uses directly: one compact "witness" value (the tree root) fixes every document in the interval at once, and any individual document’s timestamp proof shrinks to the O(log n) sibling hashes on its path to the root. The paper also suggests publishing each period’s root value somewhere public and hard to alter — the authors’ later commercial service famously printed it in a newspaper.

A Bitcoin block is this construction: transactions committed by a Merkle root in the header, the header chained to its predecessor and witnessed by the whole network’s proof-of-work. The full PDF, from co-author Dave Bayer’s Columbia page, is attached.

B59-402.001: Pricing via Processing, or Combatting Junk Mail
Cynthia Dwork & Moni Naor · CRYPTO ’92 · August 1992
“In order to send a message, the sender must compute some moderately expensive, but not intractable, function of the message and some additional information.”

This is the paper that invented proof-of-work . Long before anyone spoke of mining, Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor asked a narrow, practical question: how do you stop junk mail and the abuse of a shared resource without a central gatekeeper or a payment system?

Their answer was economic, not bureaucratic. Make the sender do a small amount of computational work — solve a “pricing function” — before a message is accepted. For a person sending a handful of messages the cost is invisible. For a spammer sending millions, the cost becomes prohibitive. Access is rationed by CPU cycles instead of identity, permission, or money.

Dwork and Naor specified pricing functions that are moderately hard to compute but easy to verify , and that can be tied to the specific message and recipient so the work can’t be pre-computed or reused. They even described a shortcut — a trapdoor the authority could use — so that the same scheme could implement more general access control.
That asymmetry — hard to produce, trivial to check, bound to its inputs — is the exact property every later system relies on.

Hashcash (Adam Back, 1997) turned the idea into a deployable email stamp. b-money (Wei Dai, 1998) and bit gold (Nick Szabo) used proof-of-work to create money . RPOW (Hal Finney, 2004) made the tokens reusable. And in 2008 Bitcoin made proof-of-work the heartbeat of a decentralized ledger. The Bitcoin whitepaper cites Dwork and Naor directly.
Every time a miner hashes a block, it is running the descendant of an idea first written down to fight spam.

We present a computational technique for combatting junk mail in particular and controlling access to a shared resource in general. The main idea is to require a user to compute a moderately hard, but not intractable, function in order to gain access to the resource, thus preventing frivolous use.

B59-402.003: Hashcash — A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
Adam Back · technical report · 1 August 2002 (“5 years on”)
A parameterisable, publicly auditable cost-function: cheap to verify, tunably expensive to compute.

Written five years after the 1997 code, this is the reference description of hashcash. Back formalises the notion of a "cost-function" — a computation that is moderately hard to perform but cheap to check — and classifies such functions as interactive or non-interactive, publicly auditable or privately verifiable, and fixed-cost or probabilistic-cost.

The hashcash function itself is a partial pre-image (partial hash collision) problem: find a stamp whose hash has k leading zero bits. The paper gives the stamp format, discusses efficiency, pre-computation and the effect of Moore’s law, and reviews uses including DoS mitigation, Hal Finney’s reusable-proof-of-work tokens, and mail postage.

The full 10-page PDF is attached as the primary source. Its argument — unforgeable, tunable, publicly verifiable cost as a Sybil / flooding counter-measure — is the mechanism Bitcoin adopts for block production.

B59-402.004: Cynthia Dwork, Andrew Goldberg and Moni Naor · Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO 2003 · August 2003
"Memory access speeds vary across machines much less than do CPU speeds, [so] memory-bound functions may behave more equitably than CPU-bound functions."

It is the missing middle of the proof-of-work story. Between the 1992 origin (B59-402.001) and Bitcoin’s 2008 hash-based mining, researchers already saw the central weakness of CPU puzzles, hardware asymmetry, and tried to fix it. The "memory-hard" and "ASIC-resistant" functions later used by Litecoin (scrypt), Ethereum (Ethash) and others are pursuing exactly the goal set here.

A formal model of a memory-bound computation, an abstract function with an asymptotically tight amortized lower bound on required memory accesses for the sender, a concrete instantiation inspired by RC4, a way for the receiver to verify with no memory accesses, and measurements showing only a 4x spread between a set-top box and a fast workstation.

The memory-hardness research line runs from here through Percival’s scrypt (2009) to Argon2 and the egalitarian-mining designs, and informs every later argument about whether proof-of-work can stay accessible to ordinary hardware.

In 1992, Dwork and Naor proposed that e-mail messages be accompanied by easy-to-check proofs of computational effort in order to discourage junk e-mail, now known as spam. They proposed specific CPU-bound functions for this purpose. Burrows suggested that, since memory access speeds vary across machines much less than do CPU speeds, memory-bound functions may behave more equitably than CPU-bound functions... we prove that, on average, the sender of a message must perform many unrelated accesses to memory, while the receiver, in order to verify the work, has to perform significantly fewer accesses.

So asks gwern in a spectacular display of hindsight.

The short answer about why it took so long is that the bit gold/Bitcoin ideas were nowhere remotely close to being as obvious gwern suggests. They required a very substantial amount of unconventional thought, not just about the security technologies gwern lists (and I’m afraid the list misses one of the biggest ones, Byzantine-resilient peer-to-peer replication), but about how to choose and put together these protocols and why. Bitcoin is not a list of cryptographic features, it’s a very complex system of interacting mathematics and protocols in pursuit of what was a very unpopular goal.

While the security technology is very far from trivial, the “why” was by far the biggest stumbling block – nearly everybody who heard the general idea thought it was a very bad idea. Myself, Wei Dai, and Hal Finney were the only people I know of who liked the idea (or in Dai’s case his related idea) enough to pursue it to any significant extent until Nakamoto (assuming Nakamoto is not really Finney or Dai). Only Finney ( RPOW ) and Nakamoto were motivated enough to actually implement such a scheme.

The “why” requires coming to an accurate understanding of the nature of two difficult and almost always misunderstood topics, namely trust and the nature of money. The overlap between cryptographic experts and libertarians who might sympathize with such a “gold bug” idea is already rather small, since most cryptographic experts earn their living in academia and share its political biases. Even among this uncommon intersection as stated very few people thought it was a good idea. Even gold bugs didn’t care for it because we already have real gold rather than mere bits and we can pay online simply by issuing digital certificates based on real gold stored in real vaults, a la the formerly popular e-gold . On top of the plethora of these misguided reactions and criticisms, there remain many open questions and arguable points about these kinds of technologies and currencies, many of which can only be settled by actually fielding them and seeing how they work in practice, both in economic and security terms.

B59-404.002: Preserved by Project B59 · ← Return to The Vault

Blockchains are all the rage. The oldest and biggest blockchain of them all is Bitcoin , which over its eight-year history so far starshipped in value from 10,000 bitcoins per pizza (before there were exchanges that priced bitcoin in traditional currencies) to over 1,000 per bitcoin. As of this writing Bitcoin has a market capitalization of over 16 billion. Running non-stop for eight years, with almost no financial loss on the chain itself, it is now in important ways the most reliable and secure financial network in the world.

The secret to Bitcoin’s success is certainly not its computational efficiency or its scalability in the consumption of resources. Specialized Bitcoin hardware is designed by highly paid experts to perform only one particular function—to repetitively solve a very specific and intentionally very expensive kind of computational puzzle. That puzzle is called a proof-of-work, because the sole output of the computation is just a proof that the computer did a costly computation. Bitcoin’s puzzle-solving hardware probably consumes in total over 500 megawatts of electricity. And that is not the only feature of Bitcoin that strikes an engineer or businessman who is focused on minimizing resource costs as highly quixotic. Rather than reduce its protocol messages to be as few as possible, each Bitcoin-running computer sprays the Internet with a redundantly large number of “inventory vector” packets to make very sure that all messages get accurately through to as many other Bitcoin computers as possible. As a result, the Bitcoin blockchain cannot process as many transactions per second as a traditional payment network such as PayPal or Visa. Bitcoin offends the sensibilities of resource-conscious and performance-measure-maximizing engineers and businessmen alike.

A smart contract is a computerized transaction protocol that executes the terms of a contract. The general objectives of smart contract design are to satisfy common contractual conditions (such as payment terms, liens, confidentiality, and even enforcement), minimize exceptions both malicious and accidental, and minimize the need for trusted intermediaries. Related economic goals include lowering fraud loss, arbitration and enforcement costs, and other transaction costs. [1]
Some technologies that exist today can be considered as crude smart contracts, for example POS terminals and cards, EDI, and agoric allocation of public network bandwidth.

Digital cash protocols [ 2 , 3 ] are fine examples of smart contracts. They enable online payment while honoring the characteristics desired of paper cash: unforgeability, confidentiality, and divisibility. When we take a second glance at digital cash protocols, considering them in the wider context of smart contract design, we see that these protocols can be used to implement a wide variety of electronic bearer securities, not just cash. We also see that to implement a full customer-vendor transaction, we need more than just the digital cash protocol; we need a protocol that guarantees that product will be delivered if payment is made, and vice versa. Current commercial systems use a wide variety of techniques to accomplish this, such as certified mail, face to face exchange, reliance on credit history and collection agencies to extend credit, etc. Smart contracts have the potential to greatly reduce the fraud and enforcement costs of many commercial transactions. Digital cash protocols use several of the rich new building blocks coming out of the fields of cryptography and computer science. Most of these components have not yet been widely exploited to facilitate contractual arrangements, but the potential is vast. These subprotocols include Byzantine agreement, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, blind signatures, cut & choose, bit commitment, multiparty secure computations , secret sharing , and oblivious transfer. All of these except the first are described in [ 2 , 3 ].
