B59-901.007: No matter what you do, players will decode every formula, statistic, and algorithm in your world via experimentation.

Koster was lead designer on Ultima Online and creative director on Star Wars Galaxies, and a heavy contributor to the MUD-Dev mailing list where much of the early MMO craft knowledge was worked out in public. This page is his attempt to compress that knowledge into aphorisms.

Several of the laws here became standard citations in their own right: "never trust the client", the observation that killing other players is structurally more rewarding than killing anything the game provides, and the argument that an online world’s community is the actual product. The list is deliberately provisional — Ola’s Law About Laws at the top invites the reader to attack each one.
Koster's book-length treatment of why games are fun, A Theory of Fun for Game Design (2003), is catalogued as a link-only reference at B59-903.004.

These are taken from both experience and from the writings of others. Most are the sort of "Duh" things that many who have done this sort of game design take for granted, but others may be less intuitive. Many of the laws here were actually stated as such by others, and not by me.
Any general law about virtual worlds should be read as a challenge rather than as a guideline. You'll learn more from attacking it than from accepting it.
The secrets to a really long-lived, goal-oriented, online game of wide appeal
- have multiple paths of advancement (individual features are nice, but making them ladders is better)
- make it easy to switch between paths of advancement (ideally, without having to start over)
- make sure the milestones in the path of advancement are clear and visible and significant (having 600 meaningless milestones doesn't help)
- ideally, make your game not have a sense of running out of significant milestones (try to make your ladder not feel finite)
You're trying to provide as many modes of expression as possible in your online world. Character classes are just modes of expression, after all.

Once you open your online world, expect to keep your team on it indefinitely. Some of these games have never closed. And closing one prematurely may result in losing the faith of your customers, damaging the prospects for other games in the same genre.
No matter what you do, someone is going to automate the process of playing your world.
B59-902.001: B59-902.001 · JOURNALISM · IN-GAME ECONOMIES & VIRTUAL PROPERTY
Julian Dibbell · The Village Voice, 23 December 1993
The commands you type into a computer are a kind of speech that doesn’t so much communicate as make things happen.

This is the piece that made the wider public take virtual communities seriously as places where something real is at stake. Dibbell was a LambdaMOO regular; when a player calling himself Mr. Bungle used a voodoo-doll program to puppet other characters through sexual violence in a public room, he watched the community try to work out what had happened and what, if anything, it could do about it.

It is a landmark for law and for design at once: it forces the questions of whether text can constitute assault, whether a MOO can have legitimate authority to expel a member, and where the line runs between a player and the person typing. The virtual town meeting it describes, and the wizard who ultimately acted alone, became reference points for every later argument about virtual-world governance.
Pairs with Pavel Curtis’s "Mudding" (B59-901.003), which describes the same MOO a year earlier, and with the virtual-property law literature at B59-902.004.

The 79th Richest Nation on Earth doesn’t exist. The population is 225,000, the hourly wage $3.42.

A decade after "A Rape in Cyberspace", Dibbell returned to virtual worlds with a different question: not what they do to community, but what they do to money. The answer was that people were quietly earning real incomes inside game economies and cashing out on eBay, and that the game companies mostly wished they would stop.

The article is the readable companion to Castronova’s working paper (B59-902.002): same $3.42 wage, same insight that a game currency with a liquid dollar exchange rate is just a currency. Dibbell’s own project of trying to out-earn his journalism by trading Ultima Online goods later became the book Play Money.
A foundational text for the later law and policy arguments over who owns virtual items and whether a EULA can extinguish that ownership.

Not long ago, a 43-year-old Wonder Bread deliveryman named John Dugger logged on to eBay and, as people sometimes do these days, bought himself a house. Not a shabby one, either. Nine rooms, three stories, rooftop patio, walls of solid stonework - it wasn't quite a castle, but it put to shame the modest redbrick ranch house Dugger came home to every weeknight after a long day stocking the supermarket shelves of Stillwater, Oklahoma. Excellent location, too; nestled at the foot of a quiet coastal hillside, the house was just a hike away from a quaint seaside village and a quick commute from two bustling cosmopolitan cities. It was perfect, in short, except for one detail: The house was imaginary.

Equally unreal were the grounds the house stood on, the ocean it overlooked, the neighboring cities, and just about everything else associated with it - except Dugger himself, the man he bought it from, and the money he shelled out. At $750, Dugger's winning bid on the property set him back more than a week's wages and was, on the face of it, an astonishing amount for what he actually bought: one very small piece of Britannia, the fantasy world in which the networked role-playing game Ultima Online unfolds.
B59-903.003: The design is the game; without it you would have a CD full of data, but no experience.

Church, a designer on Ultima Underworld, System Shock and Thief, noticed that the technical side of games evolved by sharing named techniques, while design kept reinventing itself because it had no vocabulary to pass anything on. This article is a proposal to fix that.

The formal abstract design tools it names, most famously intention (the player forms a plan the game can understand) and perceivable consequence (the world reacts, visibly, so the player learns), became standard terms in design writing and teaching. The worked analysis of why moving in Mario 64 feels good is still widely cited.
Sits alongside Costikyan "I Have No Words and I Must Design" (B59-903.002) as the other half of the late-1990s push to give game design a critical language.

What is a modern computer game made of? It fuses a technical base with a vision for the player's experience. All of the disciplines involved (design, art, audio, levels, code, and so on) work together to achieve this synthesis.

In most disciplines, industry evolution is obvious: The machines we play on are far more powerful, screens have better resolution and more colors, paint and modeling tools are more sophisticated, audio processing is faster, and sound cards are more capable. Technical issues not even in our vocabulary ten years ago are solved and research continues with essentially infinite headroom. The technical base on which games stand (game code and content creation tools) is evolving.

Across all genres and companies, we build on our own and others' past ideas to expand technical limits, learn new techniques and explore possibilities. Ignoring an anomaly or two, no single company or team would be where it is now had it been forced to work in a vacuum.

Design, on the other hand, is the least understood aspect of computer game creation. It actualizes the vision, putting art, code, levels, and sound together into what players experience, minute to minute. Clever code, beautiful art, and stunning levels don't help if they're never encountered. Design tasks determine player goals and pacing. The design is the game; without it you would have a CD full of data, but no experience.
Sadly, design is also the aspect that has had the most trouble evolving. Not enough is done

B59-904.002: Will Crowther · FORTRAN for the PDP-10 · earliest snapshot dated 11 March 1977
YOU ARE STANDING AT THE END OF A ROAD BEFORE A SMALL BRICK BUILDING. AROUND YOU IS A FOREST.

Will Crowther was a programmer at BBN who worked on the ARPANET IMPs, an expert caver, and a Dungeons and Dragons player. Around 1975-76 he combined all three into a program that let you explore a version of Mammoth Cave by typing commands: the first text adventure, and the ancestor of interactive fiction and of the adventure game as a whole.

Crowther original was nearly lost. It survived on backup tapes of Don Woods account at the Stanford AI Lab; Woods found it there around 1977 and expanded it into the 350-point version most people played. Dennis Jerz scholarship (B59-904.007) reconstructed the provenance and matched the in-game map to the real cave passages.
The archived .zip holds every recovered file: the dated main-program snapshots, the data files, and later Fortran-77 ports. The listing below is advf4.77-03-11, the earliest surviving main program.

B59-904.006: As the story goes, APh Technology Consultants (located in Pasadena, CA) was hired by Mattel in 1976 to help design what became the Intellivision system; eventually they programmed the system's software, most of the development tools, and all of the first Intellivision, M Network, and Keyboard Component games. The team consisted of APh president Glenn Hightower, graphics artist Dave James (from the Mattel Design & Development Department, who

worked with APh to define the Intellivision�s system graphics, including the familiar running-man animation), and programmers, who were graduates of the California Institute of Technology (CalTech). The name, APh, was derived from the Applied Physics courses offered at CalTech. One of those graduates was Hal Finney, who became one of the more prolific game designers there.
Q: You graduated from the California Institute of Technology with a BS in Engineering in 1979, correct? What was your first job after school?

Hal Finney: I was supposed to graduate in 1978 but I was short a few units. So I got hired full time at APh the summer of 1978 and just took the remaining classes at Caltech during that first year at APh, graduating in 1979. I continued working at APh until about 1986.
Q: When did you start at APh? Do you recall who you interviewed with?
Hal Finney: I think I was hired by Glenn Hightower , who was co-owner and the main manager at that time. I knew Dave Rolfe well, who was already working there, and he put in a good word for me.

Hal Finney: Actually I did not initially work on games at APh. My first year or so I was working on cash register software. APh had a number of consulting contracts with companies other than Mattel, although over the next few years the video game business became the largest effort of the firm.

My initial contribution to the games was creating the sound effects. The sound effect hardware on the Intellivision was primitive, but Dave Rolfe had created a sort of mini programming language to let you control it. chip talk, but it didn't really work that well. We ended up using it as the "Yer out!" sound in Major League Baseball .

B59-904.007: B59-904.007 · WRITING · GAME & ARCADE HISTORY
Dennis G. Jerz · Digital Humanities Quarterly 1:2, 2007
Will Crowther based his program on a real cave in Kentucky; Don Woods expanded this version significantly.

For thirty years the history of Adventure was told from memory and got the details wrong: dates, authorship, what Crowther wrote versus what Woods added. Jerz went back to the sources: the FORTRAN listing recovered from Woods account (catalogued here as B59-904.002), the people involved, and the cave itself.

The article establishes the record that later histories rely on: Crowther original was a smaller, less puzzle-heavy game written after his divorce, partly to share with his daughters; Woods 1977 expansion added the scoring and much of the fantasy content; and the game geography is a recognisable map of the Bedquilt entrance to Mammoth Cave, which Crowther had surveyed.
The full article, with its photographs and code excerpts, is preserved in the archived source snapshot; the opening is reproduced below.

B59-904.008: B59-904.008 · WRITING · GAME HISTORY · GAME ARTS · JAPANESE PC GAMING
Satoshi Uesaka: Game Arts and the Thexder Line
Project B59 Research · assembled 1 September 2026 · profile record, subclass 9.04 (game & arcade history)

A working credit history, not a biography: the Japanese-PC-gaming figure who did graphic and mechanical design on Thexder and Silpheed, then directed the Thexder sequel, told through his canonical dated credit list.

Class 9 of the collection covers virtual worlds and games; subclass 9.04 covers game and arcade history, the record of how the medium and its craft actually developed. Most of that subclass so far is North American: Spacewar! , Colossal Cave, the coin-op arcade, APh Technological Consulting and Intellivision. Satoshi Uesaka (上坂 哲) is a small, concrete entry from the other major branch: the Japanese home-computer scene of the mid-1980s, built on NEC's PC-8801 and its contemporaries rather than on consoles or arcade boards.

Uesaka worked at Game Arts, the Tokyo studio founded in 1985 by Yoichi and Takeshi Miyaji. Game Arts made its name with technically aggressive action games for general-purpose personal computers, and Uesaka is a representative craftsman of that period: someone who moved fluidly across graphic design, mechanical and level design, programming, and direction, on titles that were among the most demonstrated pieces of software on the PC-88. He is not a cypherpunk, a cryptographer, or an economist, and there is no claim here that he is. He is a data point in the history of the personal computer as a place where games were built by hand, which is the reason class 9 exists.

Thexder (Game Arts, NEC PC-8801, April 1985) is the anchor. It is a run-and-gun game about a robot that transforms into a jet, and it was a commercial breakout for the young studio, later licensed to Square for a Famicom conversion and ported across more than a dozen platforms. Wikipedia's infobox credits its design to Hibiki Godai and Satoshi Uesaka; secondary Japanese sources describe Uesaka's contribution as graphic and mechanical design, meaning the sprite art and the moving parts of how the game plays.
